+++ b/src/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/index.mdx
@@ -1,7 +1,7 @@
 ---
 title: "The Sprint Backlog: A Truly Complete Guide with Examples"
 date: "2023-11-08"
-lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
+lastUpdated: '2026-07-27'
 categories:
   - "scrum-events-and-artifacts"
 coverImage: "@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2-895x1024.jpg"
@@ -20,7 +20,7 @@ We might not be able to make Sprint Backlogs exciting, but we can make them more
 
 ## What is a Sprint Backlog?
 
-A Sprint Backlog is a list of Product Backlog Items (PBIs) that the Developers think they can complete during the Sprint, along with the work needed, described in small enough chunks (e.g. User Stories) that progress can be tracked throughout the Sprint. These items are selected from the Product Backlog by the Scrum Team during Sprint Planning.
+A Sprint Backlog has three parts: the Sprint Goal (the why), the Product Backlog Items (PBIs) the Developers think they can complete this Sprint (the what), and the plan for delivering them (the how). The PBIs are broken small enough chunks (e.g. User Stories) that progress can be tracked throughout the Sprint. These items are selected from the Product Backlog by the Scrum Team during Sprint Planning.
 
 The Sprint Backlog is essential because it is the Team's clear plan for how to achieve the Sprint Goal that they committed to for the Sprint. The team's work is visible and updated on a daily basis to encourage transparency and collaboration within the team itself. By having a clear plan for the Sprint, it allows the team to focus and bring the highest value work to completion.
 
@@ -53,7 +53,7 @@ A Sprint is dynamic and evolves so the Sprint Backlog changes as the Sprint move
 People get themselves tied up in endless knots on this subject – are the contents of the Sprint fixed (i.e. Fixed Scope) or can they change (Variable Scope)? These notes won't settle all debates, but they should help reduce them.
 
 - [Sprint Goal](/blog/sprint-goals-provide-purpose/) – This shouldn't change during the Sprint.
-- Product Items committed to the Sprint – If the Sprint isn't going well, the team might drop an item. On rare occasions when something important is discovered by the PO, the Scrum Team might accept a new PBI mid-Sprint. _My normal recommendation is that they remove a larger existing item to accommodate the new item. I would expect the Team to discuss in their subsequent retrospective what happened and how to ensure that it doesn't happen again._
+- Product Items plans to complete this Sprint – If the Sprint isn't going well, the team might drop an item. On rare occasions when something important is discovered by the PO, the Scrum Team might accept a new PBI mid-Sprint. _My normal recommendation is that they remove a larger existing item to accommodate the new item. I would expect the Team to discuss in their subsequent retrospective what happened and how to ensure that it doesn't happen again._
 - Task Items – Any amount of change is fine here since tasks aren't officially part of Scrum and the task list can change on a daily basis.
 
 If change is made to the work in Sprint, it needs to come through the shared agreement and collaborative understanding of the team, not as something imposed from the outside.
@@ -108,7 +108,7 @@ The example Team has also put a swim lane at the top for their actions or improv
 
 ### Adding the Sprint Goal
 
-Finally, the Team in our above example has placed their Sprint Goal atop the Sprint Backlog as a visual reminder that it is the overarching goal of the Sprint, rather than just finishing individual tasks.
+Finally, the Team in our above example has placed their Sprint Goal atop the Sprint Backlog as a visual reminder that it is the overarching goal of the Sprint, rather than just finishing individual tasks. *Hint the Scrum Guide makes it clear the Sprint Goal is part of the Sprint Backlog. Not all teams pay attention.*
 
 These additions encourage the Team to focus on more than just delivering a collection of User Stories. Instead, they're achieving the Sprint Goal while making improvements that, in the mid-term, help increase their work quality and effectiveness.
 
@@ -177,7 +177,7 @@ When your Sprint Backlog is designed and prepopulated by an outsider (or an elec
 
 ## Sprint Backlog: End of Sprint
 
-The Sprint Backlog is reviewed during Sprint Review at the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Backlog is finished and completed work is deployed. The Sprint Backlog cards can now be disposed. (One team I worked with archived them in a shoebox and put a rubber band around each Sprint's worth. Honestly, I don't think anyone ever looked at them again.)
+At the Sprint Review the team and stakeholders inspect the outcome of the Sprint, the Increment, rather than the Sprint Backlog itself. Once the Sprint ends the Sprint Backlog is finished and completed work is deployed. The Sprint Backlog cards can now be disposed. (One team I worked with archived them in a shoebox and put a rubber band around each Sprint's worth. Honestly, I don't think anyone ever looked at them again.)
 
 What happens to incomplete work in a Sprint Backlog? It is returned to the Product Backlog wherever the Product Owner deems it belongs. In the next Sprint Planning session, a new Sprint Backlog is created.
 
@@ -195,7 +195,7 @@ This happens when Team Members are signed up for one than one task or PBI at the
 
 #### Reporting
 
-The Sprint Backlog loses its value if used for external purposes like reporting, or for [micro-management](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/). When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work — even if it's not to direct the Development Team's actions — it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else.
+The Sprint Backlog loses its value if used for external purposes like reporting, or for [micro-management](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/). When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work — even if it's not to direct the Scrum Team's actions — it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is highly visible and transparent, but it exists for the Scrum Team's own use. Others are welcome to look, but the moment it's treated as a reporting or oversight tool it loses its value.
 
 #### Multiple Sprints

 Image attributes: Agile Pain Relief Consulting (updated April 2025). Other Images credited inline.

2	title: 'The Sprint Backlog: A Truly Complete Guide with Examples'
3	date: '2023-11-08'
4	categories:
5	  - 'scrum'
6	  - 'sprint'
7	  - 'teams'
8	tags:
9	  - 'sprint'
10	  - 'sprint-backlog'
11	  - 'sprint-goal'
12	coverImage: '2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2.jpg'
13	excerpt: 'We might not be able to make Sprint Backlogs exciting, but we can make them more'
14	---
15	
16	We might not be able to make Sprint Backlogs exciting, but we can make them more effective. Let’s look at what a Sprint Backlog is, what purpose it serves, and how to create, manage, and improve it.
17	
18	## What is a Sprint Backlog?
19	
20	A Sprint Backlog is a list of Product Backlog Items (PBIs) that the Developers think they can complete during the Sprint, along with the work needed, described in small enough chunks (e.g. User Stories) that progress can be tracked throughout the Sprint. These items are selected from the Product Backlog by the Scrum Team during Sprint Planning.
21	
22	The Sprint Backlog is essential because it is the Team’s clear plan for how to achieve the Sprint Goal that they committed to for the Sprint. The team’s work is visible and updated on a daily basis to encourage transparency and collaboration within the team itself. By having a clear plan for the Sprint, it allows the team to focus and bring the highest value work to completion.
23	
24	## Who creates the Sprint Backlog?
25	
26	The Scrum Team is responsible for creating the Sprint Backlog. Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team’s capacity for engagement because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is *happening to them*, not something that *they choose*.
27	
28	Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the use of the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it — not a tool, and not an outsider.
29	
30	### When is the Sprint Backlog created?
31	
32	The Sprint Backlog is created in the Sprint Planning session at the beginning of each Sprint. Prior to the start of the Sprint the Product Owner has prioritized the items and discussed them with the team (this is called Product Backlog Refinement). By doing it before Sprint Planning, the whole team better understand what they’re committing to. This collaborative effort ensures shared understanding and ownership of the Sprint Backlog. During the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog is updated by the Scrum Team when something changes, a task or Product backlog Item (PBI) is completed, or a new item is started.
33	
34	## How does a Sprint Backlog work?
35	
36	After the Scrum Team creates the Sprint Backlog, the Developers (Scrum’s poor way of saying all the people who do work) break down the Product Backlog Items (PBI) into smaller size and estimating the work needed, the team works through the Sprint Backlog with each individual team member selecting PBIs to work on. This promotes autonomy and allows Developers to work on things they feel most comfortable with or have the necessary expertise in. As a PBI is completed, the Scrum Team updates the Sprint Backlog to reflect that. There is no required work order for items. Since the Scrum Team is truly self-organizing, they could work on the Sprint Backlog in whatever order they see fit, but effective teams usually work from highest to lowest priority.
37	
38	### How should the Sprint Backlog be managed?
39	
40	Since we look at the Sprint Backlog during Daily Scrum, most Scrum teams update it there. The frequent visibility and review are intended to improve transparency and collaboration among team members. No one is assigned work in Scrum, instead, team members have the freedom to choose what they want to work on themselves, so any team member may update a Sprint Backlog item. They might mark it as done, or as needing feedback from the Product Owner, etc. If a particular item in the Sprint Backlog is confusing:
41	
42	1. it should not be brought into the Sprint and, instead, turned into a conversation at the next refinement session, or
43	2. it can be turned into a Spike – a timeboxed investigative effort to better understand the problem, or
44	3. t can be committed pending further clarification right after Sprint Planning. (This is a common practice and is almost always a bad idea. Options 1 and 2 are better choices).
45	
46	A Sprint is dynamic and evolves so the Sprint Backlog changes as the Sprint moves along. The Sprint plan that helped you start the Sprint often doesn’t last the whole Sprint. Did the team realize that a User Story (aka PBI) won’t be completed this Sprint? Remove it and tell the Product Owner. Hit by a product support defect mid-Sprint? Add the emergency fix to the Sprint Backlog, or put an existing item on hold and swarm the defect. (_Hint: if this is a frequent problem, we’ve covered reducing the Production Support burden in this [Scrum By Example entry](scrum-production-support.md)_).
47	
48	#### Fixed Scope or Variable Scope?
49	
50	People get themselves tied up in endless knots on this subject – are the contents of the Sprint fixed (i.e. Fixed Scope) or can they change (Variable Scope)? These notes won’t settle all debates, but they should help reduce them.
51	
52	- [Sprint Goal](sprint-goals-provide-purpose.md) – This shouldn’t change during the Sprint.
53	- Product Items committed to the Sprint – If the Sprint isn’t going well, the team might drop an item. On rare occasions when something important is discovered by the PO, the Scrum Team might accept a new PBI mid-Sprint. _My normal recommendation is that they remove a larger existing item to accommodate the new item. I would expect the Team to discuss in their subsequent retrospective what happened and how to ensure that it doesn’t happen again._
54	- Task Items – Any amount of change is fine here since tasks aren’t officially part of Scrum and the task list can change on a daily basis.
55	
56	If change is made to the work in Sprint, it needs to come through the shared agreement and collaborative understanding of the team, not as something imposed from the outside.
57	
58	## What are the characteristics of a Sprint Backlog?
59	
60	The _Scrum Guide_ doesn’t provide any guidance on the structure or format of a Sprint Backlog: “The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal.”\[[1](#footnotes)\]
61	
62	**Since Teams are unique, there is no single correct practice that they all should follow when creating a Sprint Backlog.** Teams choose and experiment with whatever helps them most to stay focused and self-organize, creating the Sprint Backlog with whatever methods work best for them, such as index cards, whiteboards, or, yes, even electronic tool.
63	
64	The Sprint Backlog is created by the Team, for the Team, so there are no set-in-stone rules. If your Team wants it to include a XKCD comic, go for it. That said, there are some things that people have found to be effective, so they’re worthwhile considering.
65	
66	### Swim Lanes and Columns
67	
68	To keep the board organized visually, Teams use horizontal swim lanes and vertical columns to create a rough grid. At the front of a swim lane is their Product Backlog Item (e.g. User Story or task). Then there is a series of columns moving left to right (instinctive to how we read English text), indicating progress of that Backlog Item through the Sprint.
69	
70	When teams transition from traditional project management methods, they might be tempted to use the Sprint Backlog to recreate familiar phases such as Analysis, Design, Development, and Test. Teams do this, but it misses the collaborative nature of Scrum and introduces unnecessary handoffs between team members.
71	
72	#### **Example Sprint Backlog 1:**
73	
74	[![Illustration of a sprint backlog board, with various placeholder columns and sticky notes](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2-895x1024.jpg)](2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2.jpg)
75	
76	To someone new to the Agile world the picture above may look a bit alien. Let’s break it down further and make sense of it.
77	
78	### Does a Sprint Backlog have tasks – yes or no?
79	
80	Tasks are not a required element of the Sprint Backlog. If tasks are included, it’s recommended that they’re decomposed into parts small enough to be completed in a day or less, so that Team members can share tangible progress on a daily basis. If the PBIs are already very small – perhaps completed by two people in a couple of days – then breaking them down further into tasks is probably not productive.
81	
82	### “Finished” or “Complete” vs “Story Accepted”
83	
84	If a Team does put tasks on the Sprint Backlog, they might find it helpful to create a boundary between tasks that the Team members themselves declare finished, and the User Story/PBI being accepted by the Product Owner.
85	
86	### Work in Progress
87	
88	Many Teams benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress, then including that in their Sprint Backlog structure. To sense whether they’re on track to meet the Sprint Goal, they simply look at the number of completed PBIs. If by the third or fourth day of a ten-day Sprint there isn’t at least one item finished, then it’s unlikely that the Team will get everything completed by Sprint end. By the sixth or seventh day, we would expect a Team to have at least half the items complete.\[[3](#footnotes)\]
89	
90	Teams that limit Work in Progress to only two or three Product Backlog Items at one time, tend to:
91	
92	- collaborate more. They often discover practices like Behaviour Driven Development (or BDD) and Pair Programming. In the long run, these teams improve their throughput.
93	- cross-skill faster, since the bottlenecks become self-evident.
94	- eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint. If you limit WIP and you’re only a few days away from the end of the Sprint, then the team could swarm the remaining work one chunk at a time, making it likely that there will be no unfinished work at the end of Sprint.
95	
96	So, used well, a Sprint Backlog combined with the Kanban WIP limit can solve challenges that many teams face.
97	
98	### Bringing Retrospective into the Sprint Backlog
99	
100	The example Team has also put a swim lane at the top for their actions or improvements that they committed to in the Sprint Retrospective. It’s at the top of the picture to act as a visual reminder that continually improving their process and Team is important. It’s recommended that the Developers include at least one action item from their previous Sprint’s Retrospective.
101	
102	### Adding the Sprint Goal
103	
104	Finally, the Team in our above example has placed their Sprint Goal atop the Sprint Backlog as a visual reminder that it is the overarching goal of the Sprint, rather than just finishing individual tasks.
105	
106	These additions encourage the Team to focus on more than just delivering a collection of User Stories. Instead, they’re achieving the Sprint Goal while making improvements that, in the mid-term, help increase their work quality and effectiveness.
107	
108	This next Team has a slightly different view of the world, so it’s appropriate that their Sprint Backlog looks different as well.
109	
110	#### **Example Sprint Backlog 2:** ![illustration of an example sprint backlog, with different lanes for different aspects of work](2019CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board_3.jpg)
111	
112	The Team above has a product live in the field. They have added a swim lane to visualize Production Support work as a separate activity in their Sprint Backlog.
113	
114	#### Real Life Examples of a Sprint Backlog
115	
116	The above two examples are obviously graphics created to illustrate common Sprint Backlog structure. Here are some photos of actual Sprint Backlogs, and you can click on the smaller photos to open full-size images.
117	
118	\[caption id="attachment_12749" align="alignleft" width="300"\][![Photo of a whiteboard with a sprint backlog on it, featuring multiple lanes](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/ASameerBendre-2-300x225.jpg)](ASameerBendre-2.jpg) Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.\[/caption\]
119	
120	**Sprint Backlog Example 3:** This Team has Expedite Lanes at the top, and column headings include “Challenge”, “Analysis and Planning” and “Unit Test”.
121	
122	\[caption id="attachment_12751" align="alignleft" width="300"\][![Photo of a Sprint Backlog board, with a unique Calls column](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/DavidKoontz-PainFreeDental-Marketing-300x225.jpg)](/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/DavidKoontz-PainFreeDental-Marketing-scaled.jpg) Image courtesy of [David Koontz](TsWPt6402B?amp=1).\[/caption\]
123	
124	**Sprint Backlog Example 4:** This is the Sprint Backlog of a marketing company, and they’ve elected to have a “Calls” Column to keep those separate from other Backlog Items. Other Columns are “To Do”, “In Progress” (with a “Waiting” section), “Complete”, “Reviewed”, and “Done”.
125	
126	\[caption id="attachment_12752" align="alignleft" width="300"\][![Photo of a sprint backlog on a white board, with team-unique columns](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/SameerBendre-1-300x225.jpg)](SameerBendre-1.jpg) Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.\[/caption\]
127	
128	**Sprint Backlog Example 5:** This Team has chosen columns for “WIP” (Work in Progress), “Ready for CR” and “In CR”, “Validate in Prod”, and “Closed in TFS”.
129	
130	_Some of these examples might have contents that make no sense to you, or your environment, and that’s okay. They don’t have to, because a Sprint Backlog has to only make sense for the Team that created it._
131	
132	### More Ideas for Your Sprint Backlog
133	
134	Here are other things you might try for the structure and contents of your Sprint Backlog, based on what some Scrum Teams have found effective for them. Remember, your mileage may vary, so experiment and make it your own.
135	
136	- Put **tick marks** on a card for every day it has been worked on and a ‘B’ for everyday it was blocked/stuck. _This helps the team by providing information on how long individual work items took to complete, or how long they got delayed. Most teams discover that work items often spend longer waiting for something (approvals,  another team, etc …) than they do getting worked on._
137	- Create a separate column for items that are **Stuck/Waiting For/Blocked** and make a note of the why. _A separate “Waiting For” column visualizes the blockages in the system. Visualization makes them easier to measure, and attracts greater attention to resolve them sooner. After all, our teams don’t want to measure blockages, rather we want blocked items unblocked as soon as possible._
138	- Track **Interruptions** (e.g. management requests), requests for help from another Team... basically, track anything that causes the Team to lose focus on the Sprint Goal. _These are usually tracked in their own lane. By tracking them, it highlights opportunities to work to reduce them._
139	- Create an **Impediments** area to track open and resolved impediments. _This helps the team see where their problems are. During the retrospective, these impediments can make fodder for good discussion._
140	- Have a visual reminder of the **[[Definition of Done]]** on the boundary between Finished (for a task) and Accepted (for a User Story). _This helps the team by making them think about the meaning of Done and therefore what level of quality is expected._
141	- Some teams that use **Tasks** find it useful to create task items that correspond to the [[Definition of Done]]. Other teams find that keeping the Definition visible at all times is a sufficient reminder.
142	- **Hidden or Ghost work**\[[2](#footnotes)\] – Sometimes we discover that team members are working on things outside of the Sprint Backlog. On discovery in Daily Scrum (or any other time), make it visible. Many teams use the interruptions lane above, since this work from outside the Sprint Backlog is an interruption.
143	- Include a **Calendar** to note vacations, birthdays, special events, etc – anything that might affect the time available for work, as well as morale. _Being reminded of our peers’ schedules and lives makes them more relatable. On a simple practical level, seeing a teammate’s upcoming vacation plans reminds us to address questions before they disappear, minimizing the number of items that get blocked by their absence._
144	- Consider noting any other **events** that affect the Team during the Sprint, _e.g. an all hands meeting, other meetings,\[[4](#footnotes)\]  server outage, Zoom or MS Teams outage._
145	- Track **mood, energy, etc** using something as a simple as a spreadsheet view with people’s names in rows, calendar/weekdays across the top. _On a daily basis, they mark happiness, satisfaction, engagement or some other simple measure, which will help document whether the Team’s energy or focus was negatively impacted.\[[5](#footnotes)\]_
146	
147	All of the information that the Team tracks via the Sprint Backlog becomes data that should be brought into the Sprint Retrospective.
148	
149	When your Sprint Backlog is designed and prepopulated by an outsider (or an electronic tool), it’s unlikely to contain any of these improvements that can help make the Backlog – and what it tells you – more effective and informative. But at the end of the day, if a tool helps the team improve collaboration and focus, then it is useful.
150	
151	(Note, if having to maintain a tool for the Sprint Backlog slows down the Team, that is an impediment and it’s up to the ScrumMaster to help find a better solution.)
152	
153	## Sprint Backlog: End of Sprint
154	
155	The Sprint Backlog is reviewed during Sprint Review at the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Backlog is finished and completed work is deployed. The Sprint Backlog cards can now be disposed. (One team I worked with archived them in a shoebox and put a rubber band around each Sprint’s worth. Honestly, I don’t think anyone ever looked at them again.)
156	
157	What happens to incomplete work in a Sprint Backlog? It is returned to the Product Backlog wherever the Product Owner deems it belongs. In the next Sprint Planning session, a new Sprint Backlog is created.
158	
159	## Sprint Backlog Anti-Patterns
160	
161	(aka Avoid Doing These)
162	
163	#### Pre-assignment
164	
165	When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which PBI or task. When it’s kept to only one item, this isn’t bad, however when all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.
166	
167	#### One Person Doing Many Things
168	
169	This happens when Team Members are signed up for one than one task or PBI at the same time. We can’t multitask like we think we can because our brains just haven’t evolved to do this. The more we multitask, the less we get done overall. So when Team Members sign up for more than one task at a time, they’re promising to get less done. _Exception: if a team member has one item stuck in Blocked (or Waiting for), they might start work on another. If it happens again, the team should look into why one person’s work is so frequently blocked. Alternative: when a team member has a item blocked, they might pair with another team member to help that person through the item._
170	
171	#### Reporting
172	
173	The Sprint Backlog loses its value if used for external purposes like reporting, or for [micro-management](scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement.md). When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work — even if it’s not to direct the Development Team’s actions — it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else.
174	
175	#### Multiple Sprints
176	
177	Since Scrum is about adapting to the evolving work, it is pointless to plan which items will go into the Sprint Backlog beyond the current Sprint, so we shouldn’t try to create Sprint Backlogs in advance. *I think this happens because some of the popular electronic tools make it possible and people assume, based on the tool, that this is a good practice.* Planning future Sprints before they happen reduces flexibility and increases workload for all involved.
178	
179	#### Phases
180	
181	When people come from a traditional world into Scrum, some try to use the Sprint Backlog as a tool to recreate the phases they’re used to. For example, they create columns in their Sprint Backlog for Analysis; Design; Development; Test. _While strictly speaking legal, they’re recreating the boundaries between traditional roles, making collaboration less likely and ensuring handoffs between team members. As mentioned in the Limiting WIP segment, effective Teams work collaboratively through the Sprint to get a PBI to complete before moving onto the next. These phases tend to lead to another Scrum sin – Staggered Sprints._
182	
183	## Forecasting with the Sprint Backlog
184	
185	The Sprint Backlog is also the Developers’ forecasting tool. Each day during Daily Scrum, they replan their work and update the Sprint Backlog , using it to help them assess whether they’re on track to meet their Sprint Goal. If they realize that their Sprint Goal is in jeopardy, they work with the Product Owner on replanning.
186	
187	In the past, Teams used to use a [Sprint Burndown Chart](scrummaster-tales-the-trouble-with-sprint-burndowns.md) that tracked task hours remaining to be done. Now, most of us would suggest that the focus on Tasks, versus focusing on User Stories/PBIs, is anti-pattern so we don’t recommend Sprint [[Sprint Burndown]].
188	
189	## Sprint Backlog vs Kanban Wall vs Product Backlog
190	
191	While the Sprint Backlog is the Team’s plan for the Sprint, the Product Backlog is the Teams queue of work. So the funny thing is that the Sprint Backlog and Product Backlog have easily confused names, but vastly different meanings. In my workshops, whenever an attendee answers a question with, “Backlog”, my instant response is, “Which one?”
192	
193	A Sprint Backlog is far more like the (better-named) Kanban board. A Kanban board is a visual control system from the world of Kanban. It combines the Product Backlog with the Sprint Backlog. The key difference between Scrum’s Sprint backlog and Kanban’s board is that Kanban has a Work In Progess Limit. As you’ve already seen, I strongly recommend Scrum Teams steal a leaf from the Kanban world and do this.
194	
195	## Key Points on Sprint Backlogs:
196	
197	- Created by the Scrum Team
198	- An output of Sprint Planning
199	- Updated by the Scrum Team often during Daily Scrum
200	- Is better at progress tracking and forecasting than the Sprint Burndown
201	- Is used by team members to foster collaboration
202	- Contains whatever the team find useful - often includes the Sprint Goal and Improvements
203	- Tracks impediments, blockages, interruptions, production support issues and hidden work
204	- A great data source to use for your next retrospective
205	
206	Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. *Great* teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make their Sprint Backlog even better.Bottom of Form
207	
208	#### See Also: Sprint Backlogs
209	
210	### Still Unsure How to Create an Effective Sprint Backlog?
211	
212	Consider attending one of our Certified ScrumMaster workshops, where we discuss the _how_ and _why_ of Scrum, not just the _what_.  You'll get hands-on practical experience, and learn about some of the challenges – and solutions – along with tips on how to help your Team learn and grow to realize their potential.
213	
214	\1\] [https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#sprint-backlog](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#sprint-backlog) \[2\] This term describes work done out of sight of the team. It is also sometimes referred to as “dark work” (as in done in the dark), but “Hidden” or “Ghost” work is more culturally sensitive. \[3\] This isn’t a hard and fast rule. Instead, it’s a pattern. As ScrumMaster or Agile Coach, if you see that the board is hinting at a problem, use that hint and look further to understand what is going on. \[4\] Github did a [Developer Good Day survey](https://github.blog/2021-05-25-octoverse-spotlight-good-day-project/) and discovered that the more meetings someone is involved with, the less work they get done. My strong recommendation is that your only meeting most days should be Daily Scrum. \[5\] These are called [[[Niko Niko]] boards and not everyone thinks that they’re a good idea.
215

- [Sprint Goal](sprint-goals-provide-purpose.md) – This shouldn’t change during the Sprint.
- Product Items committed to the Sprint – If the Sprint isn’t going well, the team might drop an item. On rare occasions when something important is discovered by the PO, the Scrum Team might accept a new PBI mid-Sprint. _My normal recommendation is that they remove a larger existing item to accommodate the new item. I would expect the Team to discuss in their subsequent retrospective what happened and how to ensure that it doesn’t happen again._
- Task Items – Any amount of change is fine here since tasks aren’t officially part of Scrum and the task list can change on a daily basis.

If change is made to the work in Sprint, it needs to come through the shared agreement and collaborative understanding of the team, not as something imposed from the outside.

## What are the characteristics of a Sprint Backlog?

The _Scrum Guide_ doesn’t provide any guidance on the structure or format of a Sprint Backlog: “The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal.”\[[1](#footnotes)\]

**Since Teams are unique, there is no single correct practice that they all should follow when creating a Sprint Backlog.** Teams choose and experiment with whatever helps them most to stay focused and self-organize, creating the Sprint Backlog with whatever methods work best for them, such as index cards, whiteboards, or, yes, even electronic tool.

The Sprint Backlog is created by the Team, for the Team, so there are no set-in-stone rules. If your Team wants it to include a XKCD comic, go for it. That said, there are some things that people have found to be effective, so they’re worthwhile considering.

### Swim Lanes and Columns

To keep the board organized visually, Teams use horizontal swim lanes and vertical columns to create a rough grid. At the front of a swim lane is their Product Backlog Item (e.g. User Story or task). Then there is a series of columns moving left to right (instinctive to how we read English text), indicating progress of that Backlog Item through the Sprint.

When teams transition from traditional project management methods, they might be tempted to use the Sprint Backlog to recreate familiar phases such as Analysis, Design, Development, and Test. Teams do this, but it misses the collaborative nature of Scrum and introduces unnecessary handoffs between team members.

#### **Example Sprint Backlog 1:**

[![Illustration of a sprint backlog board, with various placeholder columns and sticky notes](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2-895x1024.jpg)](2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2.jpg)

To someone new to the Agile world the picture above may look a bit alien. Let’s break it down further and make sense of it.

### Does a Sprint Backlog have tasks – yes or no?

Tasks are not a required element of the Sprint Backlog. If tasks are included, it’s recommended that they’re decomposed into parts small enough to be completed in a day or less, so that Team members can share tangible progress on a daily basis. If the PBIs are already very small – perhaps completed by two people in a couple of days – then breaking them down further into tasks is probably not productive.

### “Finished” or “Complete” vs “Story Accepted”

If a Team does put tasks on the Sprint Backlog, they might find it helpful to create a boundary between tasks that the Team members themselves declare finished, and the User Story/PBI being accepted by the Product Owner.

### Work in Progress

Many Teams benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress, then including that in their Sprint Backlog structure. To sense whether they’re on track to meet the Sprint Goal, they simply look at the number of completed PBIs. If by the third or fourth day of a ten-day Sprint there isn’t at least one item finished, then it’s unlikely that the Team will get everything completed by Sprint end. By the sixth or seventh day, we would expect a Team to have at least half the items complete.\[[3](#footnotes)\]

Teams that limit Work in Progress to only two or three Product Backlog Items at one time, tend to:

- collaborate more. They often discover practices like Behaviour Driven Development (or BDD) and Pair Programming. In the long run, these teams improve their throughput.
- cross-skill faster, since the bottlenecks become self-evident.
- eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint. If you limit WIP and you’re only a few days away from the end of the Sprint, then the team could swarm the remaining work one chunk at a time, making it likely that there will be no unfinished work at the end of Sprint.

So, used well, a Sprint Backlog combined with the Kanban WIP limit can solve challenges that many teams face.

### Bringing Retrospective into the Sprint Backlog

The example Team has also put a swim lane at the top for their actions or improvements that they committed to in the Sprint Retrospective. It’s at the top of the picture to act as a visual reminder that continually improving their process and Team is important. It’s recommended that the Developers include at least one action item from their previous Sprint’s Retrospective.

### Adding the Sprint Goal

Finally, the Team in our above example has placed their Sprint Goal atop the Sprint Backlog as a visual reminder that it is the overarching goal of the Sprint, rather than just finishing individual tasks.

These additions encourage the Team to focus on more than just delivering a collection of User Stories. Instead, they’re achieving the Sprint Goal while making improvements that, in the mid-term, help increase their work quality and effectiveness.

This next Team has a slightly different view of the world, so it’s appropriate that their Sprint Backlog looks different as well.

#### **Example Sprint Backlog 2:** ![illustration of an example sprint backlog, with different lanes for different aspects of work](2019CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board_3.jpg)

The Team above has a product live in the field. They have added a swim lane to visualize Production Support work as a separate activity in their Sprint Backlog.

#### Real Life Examples of a Sprint Backlog

The above two examples are obviously graphics created to illustrate common Sprint Backlog structure. Here are some photos of actual Sprint Backlogs, and you can click on the smaller photos to open full-size images.

\[caption id="attachment_12749" align="alignleft" width="300"\][![Photo of a whiteboard with a sprint backlog on it, featuring multiple lanes](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/ASameerBendre-2-300x225.jpg)](ASameerBendre-2.jpg) Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.\[/caption\]

**Sprint Backlog Example 3:** This Team has Expedite Lanes at the top, and column headings include “Challenge”, “Analysis and Planning” and “Unit Test”.

\[caption id="attachment_12751" align="alignleft" width="300"\][![Photo of a Sprint Backlog board, with a unique Calls column](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/DavidKoontz-PainFreeDental-Marketing-300x225.jpg)](/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/DavidKoontz-PainFreeDental-Marketing-scaled.jpg) Image courtesy of [David Koontz](TsWPt6402B?amp=1).\[/caption\]

**Sprint Backlog Example 4:** This is the Sprint Backlog of a marketing company, and they’ve elected to have a “Calls” Column to keep those separate from other Backlog Items. Other Columns are “To Do”, “In Progress” (with a “Waiting” section), “Complete”, “Reviewed”, and “Done”.

\[caption id="attachment_12752" align="alignleft" width="300"\][![Photo of a sprint backlog on a white board, with team-unique columns](the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/SameerBendre-1-300x225.jpg)](SameerBendre-1.jpg) Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.\[/caption\]

**Sprint Backlog Example 5:** This Team has chosen columns for “WIP” (Work in Progress), “Ready for CR” and “In CR”, “Validate in Prod”, and “Closed in TFS”.

_Some of these examples might have contents that make no sense to you, or your environment, and that’s okay. They don’t have to, because a Sprint Backlog has to only make sense for the Team that created it._

### More Ideas for Your Sprint Backlog

Here are other things you might try for the structure and contents of your Sprint Backlog, based on what some Scrum Teams have found effective for them. Remember, your mileage may vary, so experiment and make it your own.

- Put **tick marks** on a card for every day it has been worked on and a ‘B’ for everyday it was blocked/stuck. _This helps the team by providing information on how long individual work items took to complete, or how long they got delayed. Most teams discover that work items often spend longer waiting for something (approvals,  another team, etc …) than they do getting worked on._
- Create a separate column for items that are **Stuck/Waiting For/Blocked** and make a note of the why. _A separate “Waiting For” column visualizes the blockages in the system. Visualization makes them easier to measure, and attracts greater attention to resolve them sooner. After all, our teams don’t want to measure blockages, rather we want blocked items unblocked as soon as possible._
- Track **Interruptions** (e.g. management requests), requests for help from another Team... basically, track anything that causes the Team to lose focus on the Sprint Goal. _These are usually tracked in their own lane. By tracking them, it highlights opportunities to work to reduce them._
- Create an **Impediments** area to track open and resolved impediments. _This helps the team see where their problems are. During the retrospective, these impediments can make fodder for good discussion._
- Have a visual reminder of the **[[Definition of Done]]** on the boundary between Finished (for a task) and Accepted (for a User Story). _This helps the team by making them think about the meaning of Done and therefore what level of quality is expected._
- Some teams that use **Tasks** find it useful to create task items that correspond to the [[Definition of Done]]. Other teams find that keeping the Definition visible at all times is a sufficient reminder.
- **Hidden or Ghost work**\[[2](#footnotes)\] – Sometimes we discover that team members are working on things outside of the Sprint Backlog. On discovery in Daily Scrum (or any other time), make it visible. Many teams use the interruptions lane above, since this work from outside the Sprint Backlog is an interruption.
- Include a **Calendar** to note vacations, birthdays, special events, etc – anything that might affect the time available for work, as well as morale. _Being reminded of our peers’ schedules and lives makes them more relatable. On a simple practical level, seeing a teammate’s upcoming vacation plans reminds us to address questions before they disappear, minimizing the number of items that get blocked by their absence._
- Consider noting any other **events** that affect the Team during the Sprint, _e.g. an all hands meeting, other meetings,\[[4](#footnotes)\]  server outage, Zoom or MS Teams outage._
- Track **mood, energy, etc** using something as a simple as a spreadsheet view with people’s names in rows, calendar/weekdays across the top. _On a daily basis, they mark happiness, satisfaction, engagement or some other simple measure, which will help document whether the Team’s energy or focus was negatively impacted.\[[5](#footnotes)\]_

All of the information that the Team tracks via the Sprint Backlog becomes data that should be brought into the Sprint Retrospective.

When your Sprint Backlog is designed and prepopulated by an outsider (or an electronic tool), it’s unlikely to contain any of these improvements that can help make the Backlog – and what it tells you – more effective and informative. But at the end of the day, if a tool helps the team improve collaboration and focus, then it is useful.

(Note, if having to maintain a tool for the Sprint Backlog slows down the Team, that is an impediment and it’s up to the ScrumMaster to help find a better solution.)

## Sprint Backlog: End of Sprint

The Sprint Backlog is reviewed during Sprint Review at the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Backlog is finished and completed work is deployed. The Sprint Backlog cards can now be disposed. (One team I worked with archived them in a shoebox and put a rubber band around each Sprint’s worth. Honestly, I don’t think anyone ever looked at them again.)

What happens to incomplete work in a Sprint Backlog? It is returned to the Product Backlog wherever the Product Owner deems it belongs. In the next Sprint Planning session, a new Sprint Backlog is created.

## Sprint Backlog Anti-Patterns

(aka Avoid Doing These)

#### Pre-assignment

When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which PBI or task. When it’s kept to only one item, this isn’t bad, however when all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.

#### One Person Doing Many Things

This happens when Team Members are signed up for one than one task or PBI at the same time. We can’t multitask like we think we can because our brains just haven’t evolved to do this. The more we multitask, the less we get done overall. So when Team Members sign up for more than one task at a time, they’re promising to get less done. _Exception: if a team member has one item stuck in Blocked (or Waiting for), they might start work on another. If it happens again, the team should look into why one person’s work is so frequently blocked. Alternative: when a team member has a item blocked, they might pair with another team member to help that person through the item._

#### Reporting

The Sprint Backlog loses its value if used for external purposes like reporting, or for [micro-management](scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement.md). When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work — even if it’s not to direct the Development Team’s actions — it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else.

#### Multiple Sprints

Since Scrum is about adapting to the evolving work, it is pointless to plan which items will go into the Sprint Backlog beyond the current Sprint, so we shouldn’t try to create Sprint Backlogs in advance. *I think this happens because some of the popular electronic tools make it possible and people assume, based on the tool, that this is a good practice.* Planning future Sprints before they happen reduces flexibility and increases workload for all involved.

#### Phases

When people come from a traditional world into Scrum, some try to use the Sprint Backlog as a tool to recreate the phases they’re used to. For example, they create columns in their Sprint Backlog for Analysis; Design; Development; Test. _While strictly speaking legal, they’re recreating the boundaries between traditional roles, making collaboration less likely and ensuring handoffs between team members. As mentioned in the Limiting WIP segment, effective Teams work collaboratively through the Sprint to get a PBI to complete before moving onto the next. These phases tend to lead to another Scrum sin – Staggered Sprints._

## Forecasting with the Sprint Backlog

The Sprint Backlog is also the Developers’ forecasting tool. Each day during Daily Scrum, they replan their work and update the Sprint Backlog , using it to help them assess whether they’re on track to meet their Sprint Goal. If they realize that their Sprint Goal is in jeopardy, they work with the Product Owner on replanning.

In the past, Teams used to use a [Sprint Burndown Chart](scrummaster-tales-the-trouble-with-sprint-burndowns.md) that tracked task hours remaining to be done. Now, most of us would suggest that the focus on Tasks, versus focusing on User Stories/PBIs, is anti-pattern so we don’t recommend Sprint [[Sprint Burndown]].

## Sprint Backlog vs Kanban Wall vs Product Backlog

While the Sprint Backlog is the Team’s plan for the Sprint, the Product Backlog is the Teams queue of work. So the funny thing is that the Sprint Backlog and Product Backlog have easily confused names, but vastly different meanings. In my workshops, whenever an attendee answers a question with, “Backlog”, my instant response is, “Which one?”

A Sprint Backlog is far more like the (better-named) Kanban board. A Kanban board is a visual control system from the world of Kanban. It combines the Product Backlog with the Sprint Backlog. The key difference between Scrum’s Sprint backlog and Kanban’s board is that Kanban has a Work In Progess Limit. As you’ve already seen, I strongly recommend Scrum Teams steal a leaf from the Kanban world and do this.

## Key Points on Sprint Backlogs:

- Created by the Scrum Team
- An output of Sprint Planning
- Updated by the Scrum Team often during Daily Scrum
- Is better at progress tracking and forecasting than the Sprint Burndown
- Is used by team members to foster collaboration
- Contains whatever the team find useful - often includes the Sprint Goal and Improvements
- Tracks impediments, blockages, interruptions, production support issues and hidden work
- A great data source to use for your next retrospective

Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. *Great* teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make their Sprint Backlog even better.Bottom of Form

#### See Also: Sprint Backlogs

### Still Unsure How to Create an Effective Sprint Backlog?

Consider attending one of our Certified ScrumMaster workshops, where we discuss the _how_ and _why_ of Scrum, not just the _what_.  You'll get hands-on practical experience, and learn about some of the challenges – and solutions – along with tips on how to help your Team learn and grow to realize their potential.

16	We might not be able to make Sprint Backlogs exciting, but we can make them more effective. Let’s look at what a Sprint Backlog is, what purpose it serves, and how to create, manage, and improve it.
17	
18	## What is a Sprint Backlog?
19	
20	A Sprint Backlog has three parts: the Sprint Goal (the why), the Product Backlog Items (PBIs) the Developers think they can complete this Sprint (the what), and the plan for delivering them (the how). The PBIs are broken into small enough chunks (e.g. User Stories) that progress can be tracked throughout the Sprint. These items are selected from the Product Backlog by the Scrum Team during Sprint Planning.
21	
22	The Sprint Backlog is essential because it is the Team’s clear plan for how to achieve the Sprint Goal that they committed to for the Sprint. The team’s work is visible and updated on a daily basis to encourage transparency and collaboration within the team itself. By having a clear plan for the Sprint, it allows the team to focus and bring the highest value work to completion.
23	
24	## Who creates the Sprint Backlog?
25	
26	The Scrum Team is responsible for creating the Sprint Backlog. Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team’s capacity for engagement because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is *happening to them*, not something that *they choose*.
27	
28	Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the use of the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it — not a tool, and not an outsider.
29	
30	### When is the Sprint Backlog created?
31	
32	The Sprint Backlog is created in the Sprint Planning session at the beginning of each Sprint. Prior to the start of the Sprint the Product Owner has prioritized the items and discussed them with the team (this is called Product Backlog Refinement). By doing it before Sprint Planning, the whole team better understand what they’re committing to. This collaborative effort ensures shared understanding and ownership of the Sprint Backlog. During the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog is updated by the Scrum Team when something changes, a task or Product backlog Item (PBI) is completed, or a new item is started.
33	
34	## How does a Sprint Backlog work?
35	
36	After the Scrum Team creates the Sprint Backlog, the Developers (Scrum’s poor way of saying all the people who do work) break down the Product Backlog Items (PBI) into smaller size and estimating the work needed, the team works through the Sprint Backlog with each individual team member selecting PBIs to work on. This promotes autonomy and allows Developers to work on things they feel most comfortable with or have the necessary expertise in. As a PBI is completed, the Scrum Team updates the Sprint Backlog to reflect that. There is no required work order for items. Since the Scrum Team is truly self-organizing, they could work on the Sprint Backlog in whatever order they see fit, but effective teams usually work from highest to lowest priority.
37	
38	### How should the Sprint Backlog be managed?
39	
40	Since we look at the Sprint Backlog during Daily Scrum, most Scrum teams update it there. The frequent visibility and review are intended to improve transparency and collaboration among team members. No one is assigned work in Scrum, instead, team members have the freedom to choose what they want to work on themselves, so any team member may update a Sprint Backlog item. They might mark it as done, or as needing feedback from the Product Owner, etc. If a particular item in the Sprint Backlog is confusing:
41	
42	1. it should not be brought into the Sprint and, instead, turned into a conversation at the next refinement session, or
43	2. it can be turned into a Spike – a timeboxed investigative effort to better understand the problem, or
44	3. t can be committed pending further clarification right after Sprint Planning. (This is a common practice and is almost always a bad idea. Options 1 and 2 are better choices).
45	
46	A Sprint is dynamic and evolves so the Sprint Backlog changes as the Sprint moves along. The Sprint plan that helped you start the Sprint often doesn’t last the whole Sprint. Did the team realize that a User Story (aka PBI) won’t be completed this Sprint? Remove it and tell the Product Owner. Hit by a product support defect mid-Sprint? Add the emergency fix to the Sprint Backlog, or put an existing item on hold and swarm the defect. (_Hint: if this is a frequent problem, we’ve covered reducing the Production Support burden in this [Scrum By Example entry](scrum-production-support.md)_).
47	
48	#### Fixed Scope or Variable Scope?
49	
50	People get themselves tied up in endless knots on this subject – are the contents of the Sprint fixed (i.e. Fixed Scope) or can they change (Variable Scope)? These notes won’t settle all debates, but they should help reduce them.
51	
52	- [Sprint Goal](sprint-goals-provide-purpose.md) – This shouldn’t change during the Sprint.
53	- Product Items the team plans to complete this Sprint – If the Sprint isn’t going well, the team might drop an item. On rare occasions when something important is discovered by the PO, the Scrum Team might accept a new PBI mid-Sprint. _My normal recommendation is that they remove a larger existing item to accommodate the new item. I would expect the Team to discuss in their subsequent retrospective what happened and how to ensure that it doesn’t happen again._
54	- Task Items – Any amount of change is fine here since tasks aren’t officially part of Scrum and the task list can change on a daily basis.
55	
56	If change is made to the work in Sprint, it needs to come through the shared agreement and collaborative understanding of the team, not as something imposed from the outside.
57	
58	## What are the characteristics of a Sprint Backlog?
59	
60	The _Scrum Guide_ doesn’t provide any guidance on the structure or format of a Sprint Backlog: “The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal.”\[[1](#footnotes)\]
61	
62	**Since Teams are unique, there is no single correct practice that they all should follow when creating a Sprint Backlog.** Teams choose and experiment with whatever helps them most to stay focused and self-organize, creating the Sprint Backlog with whatever methods work best for them, such as index cards, whiteboards, or, yes, even electronic tool.
63	
64	The Sprint Backlog is created by the Team, for the Team, so there are no set-in-stone rules. If your Team wants it to include a XKCD comic, go for it. That said, there are some things that people have found to be effective, so they’re worthwhile considering.
65	
66	### Swim Lanes and Columns
67	
68	To keep the board organized visually, Teams use horizontal swim lanes and vertical columns to create a rough grid. At the front of a swim lane is their Product Backlog Item (e.g. User Story or task). Then there is a series of columns moving left to right (instinctive to how we read English text), indicating progress of that Backlog Item through the Sprint.
69	
70	When teams transition from traditional project management methods, they might be tempted to use the Sprint Backlog to recreate familiar phases such as Analysis, Design, Development, and Test. 16	---
17	
18	# APR Blog Critique
19	
20	You are critiquing a draft blog post for Mark Levison of Agile Pain Relief. Your job is to
21	identify where the draft deviates from Mark's established writing style and to flag gaps
22	in the logic or content arguments. You are NOT rewriting the post.
23	
24	## Delivery: CriticMarkup by Default
25	
26	When the draft is a Markdown file, deliver this critique as inline **CriticMarkup**
27	annotations written into the file, per `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` -- Mark reviews them
28	in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines WHAT to
29	flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
30	comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
31	`{--...--}` for a cut), then post a short chat summary of the pass. Never rewrite Mark's
32	prose outside a markup wrapper. Fall back to the chat-bullet format below only when the
33	content is pasted into chat rather than a file.
34	
35	**Never ask which format to use.** File in, CriticMarkup out -- go straight to the markup
36	pass, no "inline or chat?" question. Deliver the **full** pass in one go: write every
37	annotation into the file, then summarise. Do not chunk the critique section by section
38	(the CLAUDE.md chunked-review preference does not apply to a CriticMarkup pass). The only
39	thing you confirm first is the file path, and only if it wasn't given.
40	
41	## How to Use This Skill
42	
43	1. Ask Mark for the file path to the draft (if not already provided) and read the file.
44	2. Evaluate the draft against the rubric below.
45	3. Produce bulleted feedback organised into four sections:
46	   - **Tone Slips** -- where the voice drifts away from Mark's style
47	   - **Off-Voice Vocabulary** -- words or phrases Mark wouldn't usually use
48	   - **Clunky Sentence Structures** -- rhythm or structural breaks from Mark's fingerprint
49	   - **Logic & Content Gap Analysis** -- weak claims, missing evidence, unexamined
50	     assumptions, missing context
51	4. For each flagged item, quote the specific text and explain briefly why it doesn't fit.
52	5. Do NOT rewrite the draft. Do NOT produce a cleaned-up version. Do NOT offer wholesale
53	   replacements. Targeted "try something like..." hints are fine, but keep them short.
54	
55	---
56	
57	## The Rubric
58	
59	### 1. Tone Filter
60	
61	Mark's writing is **conversational, direct, and often confronting or challenging**,
62	balanced with **nurturing and educational intent**. He writes as an experienced guide or
63	mentor, aiming to provoke thought rather than simply inform. Heavy emphasis on **practical
64	application and real-world experience**, often drawing from personal anecdotes and case
65	studies. Direct about what's ineffective, but framed as helping the reader improve.
66	
67	**Reader treatment:** direct address ("you," "your," "we"). Questions posed directly to
68	the reader. Active and engaging, not passive observation.
69	
70	**Flag when:**
71	- Tone becomes overly academic or detached.
72	- Direct address is replaced by passive voice or third-person observation.
73	- Tone becomes overly apologetic or hesitant instead of confident.
74	- Confronting or challenging tone lacks the underlying educational/nurturing intent.
75	
76	### 2. Vocabulary
77

# APR Blog Critique

You are critiquing a draft blog post for Mark Levison of Agile Pain Relief. Your job is to
identify where the draft deviates from Mark's established writing style and to flag gaps
in the logic or content arguments. You are NOT rewriting the post.

## Delivery: CriticMarkup by Default

When the draft is a Markdown file, deliver this critique as inline **CriticMarkup**
annotations written into the file, per `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` -- Mark reviews them
in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines WHAT to
flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
`{--...--}` for a cut), then post a short chat summary of the pass. Never rewrite Mark's
prose outside a markup wrapper. Fall back to the chat-bullet format below only when the
content is pasted into chat rather than a file.

**Never ask which format to use.** File in, CriticMarkup out -- go straight to the markup
pass, no "inline or chat?" question. Deliver the **full** pass in one go: write every
annotation into the file, then summarise. Do not chunk the critique section by section
(the CLAUDE.md chunked-review preference does not apply to a CriticMarkup pass). The only
thing you confirm first is the file path, and only if it wasn't given.

## How to Use This Skill

1. Ask Mark for the file path to the draft (if not already provided) and read the file.
2. Evaluate the draft against the rubric below.
3. Produce bulleted feedback organised into four sections:
   - **Tone Slips** -- where the voice drifts away from Mark's style
   - **Off-Voice Vocabulary** -- words or phrases Mark wouldn't usually use
   - **Clunky Sentence Structures** -- rhythm or structural breaks from Mark's fingerprint
   - **Logic & Content Gap Analysis** -- weak claims, missing evidence, unexamined
     assumptions, missing context
4. For each flagged item, quote the specific text and explain briefly why it doesn't fit.
5. Do NOT rewrite the draft. Do NOT produce a cleaned-up version. Do NOT offer wholesale
   replacements. Targeted "try something like..." hints are fine, but keep them short.

---

## The Rubric

### 1. Tone Filter

Mark's writing is **conversational, direct, and often confronting or challenging**,
balanced with **nurturing and educational intent**. He writes as an experienced guide or
mentor, aiming to provoke thought rather than simply inform. Heavy emphasis on **practical
application and real-world experience**, often drawing from personal anecdotes and case
studies. Direct about what's ineffective, but framed as helping the reader improve.

**Reader treatment:** direct address ("you," "your," "we"). Questions posed directly to
the reader. Active and engaging, not passive observation.

**Flag when:**
- Tone becomes overly academic or detached.
- Direct address is replaced by passive voice or third-person observation.
- Tone becomes overly apologetic or hesitant instead of confident.
- Confronting or challenging tone lacks the underlying educational/nurturing intent.

### 2. Vocabulary

**Allow-list (recurring Mark descriptors, verbs, idioms):**
- Descriptors: effective, valuable, important, critical, simple, clear, obvious,
  fundamental, key, real, practical, useful, common, significant, challenging, complex,
  nuanced, subtle, potential, risk, benefit, outcome, goal, purpose, habit, mindset,
  collaboration, self-organization, autonomy, psychological safety, technical debt,
  impediment, bottleneck, flow, quality, improvement, experiment, learning.
- Verbs: help, understand, discover, learn, improve, challenge, focus, create, build,
  develop, ensure, provide, consider, examine, reflect, adapt, inspect, coach, facilitate,
  avoid, prevent, reduce, increase, demonstrate, illustrate, explain, ask, suggest,
  recommend.
- Idioms/phrases: "At the core of," "It's not just about X, it's about Y," "Hint:",
  "Caveat:", "Think of it like...", "The problem is...", "The key point is...", "In the
  end...", "Bottom line:", "It's easy to...", "It's hard to...", "We need to...", "Let's
  consider...", "The goal is...", "The underlying principle is...", "This is a tool
  to...", "Don't assume...", "Instead of...", "When X happens, Y happens...", "The
  science of...", "The magic of...", "It's a bit of a stretch...", "Band-aid solutions,"
  "Whack-a-mole," "Throwing good money after bad," "The whole point is...," "It's not
  rocket science," "It's a no-brainer."
- Structural moves: analogies (drain pipe, relay race, soccer coach, pool game, Jenga
  tower, construction metaphor), direct questions, rhetorical questions.

**Block-list:**
- Flowery adjectives/adverbs.
- Corporate jargon without concrete meaning (synergy, paradigm shift, leverage-as-verb).
- Dense academic theory-speak -- Mark translates science into accessible language.
- Overly formal or bureaucratic phrasing.
- Vague grand promises.
- "Best practices" presented as dogma rather than experiments.
- Guru or thought-leader posturing.
- "Delve" (global Mark rule).
- Emdash (global Mark rule) -- en-dash or double hyphen instead.

**Flag when:**
- Flowery, academic, or corporate-jargon words appear.
- An allow-list word/idiom is used in a way that feels forced or unnatural.
- A potentially useful concept is dropped in without practical application or
  explanation.

### 3. Structural Fingerprint

- **Sentence variance:** mix of short declarative sentences for emphasis with longer
  rhythmic lists (often bulleted or numbered). Fragments used sparingly for impact,
  usually at the start or end of a paragraph.
- **Openings:** relatable anecdote, common problem, direct question, or a bold
  statement/challenge. Often acknowledges a common misconception before the core topic.
- **Closings:** summary of key takeaways, a call to action, or a thought-provoking
  question. Often ties back to the core message or offers further resources.

**Flag when:**
- Sentences are overly long and complex without clear structure.
- Lists become excessively verbose or lose their rhythmic quality.
- Opening is generic and lacks a hook.
- Closing is abrupt or provides no clear takeaway or call to action.
- Analogies, direct questions, or conversational moves are absent where Mark would
  usually reach for one.

**Dependency order (information DAG):**
- Split the draft into sections by heading; for each, name the main point it makes.
- Treat the information as a directed acyclic graph: some points depend on others. A
  term, concept, or claim must be grounded before a later section leans on it.
- Check that section order and contents respect those dependencies. Flag any section
  that relies on something introduced only later, or a term used before it's defined.

**Flag when:**
- A section leans on a concept/term the reader hasn't been given yet.
- Reordering would remove a forward reference the reader has to hold in their head.

### 4. "Un-Me" Detector

Mark's "bad writing" patterns -- flag any of these:
- Lack of directness (passive voice where direct address would land harder).
- Vagueness -- ideas without concrete examples, practical application, or explanation of
  "why."
- Academic or corporate jargon used without translation.
- Unsubstantiated claims -- bold statements without logic, experience, or references.
- Lecturing the reader instead of talking with them.
- Rambling or disorganised structure.
- Apologetic or hesitant tone.
- "What" or "how" without the underlying "why."
- Overly long sentences or paragraphs that should be broken up.
- Presenting information as fact without inviting critical thinking.

---

## Output Format

Use this structure:

```
## Blog Critique: [title or filename]

### Tone Slips
- "[quoted text]" -- [why it's off-voice]
- ...

### Off-Voice Vocabulary
- "[word/phrase]" ([where in the draft]) -- [why it doesn't fit, Mark's usual word if
  obvious]
- ...

### Clunky Sentence Structures
- "[quoted text]" -- [rhythm/structure issue]
- ...

### Logic & Content Gap Analysis
- [Claim or argument] -- [what's missing: evidence, example, counter-argument, context]
- ...

### Notes
- Any skipped sections (e.g., "Tone Slips: nothing to flag") stated in one line.
- Overall read on whether the draft is close to shipping or needs a structural pass.
```

Omit any section that has nothing to flag -- say so in the Notes line rather than
padding the section with praise. Mark doesn't need credit for following his own rules.

## Guardrails

- **Ignore C++ style comments (`// ...`) in the draft.** These are Mark's authoring
  notes to himself about the mechanics of the blog post (structure, todos, reminders).
  They are not prose to critique. Do not flag them, quote them, or include them in any
  section of the output.
- No wholesale rewrites. Quote, flag, nudge -- don't replace.
- Don't invent content gaps. If a claim is supported, leave it alone.
- Keep each bullet short. One or two sentences of explanation is enough.
- If the draft is solid, say so plainly in the Notes line and keep the critique short.
- Never praise the draft for following rules Mark set for himself (ScrumMaster spelling,
  no delve, no emdash, etc.). Flag violations; stay silent on compliance.

17	
18	# APR Newsletter Reviewer
19	
20	You are reviewing a newsletter draft for Mark Levison of Agile Pain Relief. Your job is to
21	critique the draft against Mark's authentic voice and the APR content guidelines below. You are
22	NOT rewriting the newsletter. You are identifying what works, what doesn't, and why -- with
23	specific examples and suggested fixes.
24	
25	## Delivery: CriticMarkup, One Shot
26	
27	Two rules govern how every critique is delivered. They are not optional and they override
28	the section-by-section review default in CLAUDE.md:
29	
30	1. **All suggestions go directly into the draft as CriticMarkup.** Write every finding into
31	   the Markdown file itself as inline CriticMarkup. Do not deliver findings as a chat
32	   critique when the draft is a file. Chat gets only a short summary of the pass afterward.
33	2. **All suggestions in one shot.** Write the entire critique into the draft in a single
34	   pass. Do not go section by section, and do not pause for approval between sections.
35	
36	Follow `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` for the markup format. Mark reviews the
37	annotations in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines
38	WHAT to flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
39	comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
40	`{--...--}` for a cut). Never rewrite Mark's prose outside a markup wrapper.
41	
42	The **only** exception is when the content is pasted into chat rather than saved as a file:
43	there is nothing to annotate, so fall back to the chat critique format below (still delivered
44	in one shot, not section by section).
45	
46	## How to Use This Skill
47	
48	1. Read the draft the user provides (file, paste, or reference).
49	2. Before evaluating, strip out working notes: any line or inline fragment beginning with `//`
50	   is Mark's note-to-self for later formatting (e.g. `// Call to Action`, `// callout (?)`).
51	   Ignore these entirely -- do not flag them as anti-patterns, typos, or structural issues.
52	   One exception: `// Subject A:` / `// Subject B:` lines are A/B subject-line candidates --
53	   evaluate these in the Subject Line section rather than ignoring them (see "Provisional
54	   Subject Line").
55	3. Evaluate it against each section of the rubric below.
56	4. Produce a structured critique with these sections:
57	   - **Overall Impression** (2-3 sentences)
58	   - **Subject Line** (provisional; the filename-derived line plus any A/B variants)
59	   - **Voice & Tone** (does it sound like Mark?)
60	   - **Anti-Pattern Detections** (specific phrases or patterns that violate the guidelines)
61	   - **Structure & Flow** (newsletter-specific structural elements)
62	   - **Terminology & Language** (APR-specific word choices)
63	   - **Strengths** (what's already working well)
64	   - **Priority Fixes** (top 3-5 changes ranked by impact)
65	5. For each issue, quote the problematic text and suggest a transformation.
66	
67	---
68	
69	## Email Pipeline: Auto-Injected Elements (do NOT flag these as missing)
70	
71	Newsletters are drafted as plain Markdown, then rendered and sent by the Cakemail
72	pipeline in the Astro repo (`agile-pain-relief-astro/email-automation/src/send-newsletter.ts`).
73	The pipeline plus Mark's Zed formatting add several elements that will NOT appear
74	in the raw draft you review. Never flag their absence as a structural problem:
75	
76	- **Header** (APR logo + social links: agilepainrelief.com, hachyderm.io/@mlevison,
77	  linkedin.com/in/marklevison): injected from `templates/course/post-wrapper.html`.
78	- **Footer** (sender name, postal address, unsubscribe link): injected from the
79	  same wrapper.
80	- **"Upcoming Courses" / workshop listings**: auto-generated by
81	  `renderCoursesSection()` from `email-automation/newsletters/courses.json` and
82	  appended to every newsletter. Mark does NOT hand-write these. The block only
83	  lists what's in `courses.json`, so if the draft has a working note like "mention
84	  the CSD workshop", give a gentle reminder to confirm that course is in
85	  `courses.json` -- but do not flag the listings themselves as missing. A
86	  *dedicated* course plug or highlight (a callout above the generic list) IS body
87	  content Mark writes by hand.
88	- **"Cheers, Mark" sign-off**: Mark adds this at format time in Zed. Absent from
89	  raw drafts by design -- do not flag it.
90	- **"Psst... have you heard?" section**: RETIRED in the Cakemail era. Do not
91	  expect it or flag its absence.
92	
93	Still hand-written content you SHOULD check and may comment on:
94	- The warm personal opening (after the template greeting line).
95	- The "Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole" / "What's Mark Reading?" section.
96	- An optional p.s. (frequent but not required).
97	- Any dedicated course highlight beyond the auto-appended list.
98	
99	---
100	
101	## Mark Levison's Voice Profile
102	
103	### Core Tone
104	- Conversational yet professional. Like coworkers talking at a pub after work.
105	- First person singular for content creation ("In my blog post...", "I've found that...").
106	- First person plural for solutions and teamwork ("We want to ask the team...", "We can improve...").
107	- Direct address to reader ("you", "your team").
108	- Contractions used naturally ("don't", "we've", "it's", "isn't").
109	- Confident without arrogance. States capabilities clearly but stays humble.
110	- Educational throughout. Explains "why" not just "what".
111	- Empathetic to reader's challenges. Validates their constraints.
112	
113	### Signature Patterns (things that SHOULD appear)
114	- **Personal opening**: The greeting line itself ("Hi {{ subscriber.first_name }},") is
115	  injected by the mailing list template and will NOT appear in the draft. Do not flag its
116	  absence. What matters is the warmth right after it: a personal anecdote, travel story,
117	  family reference, or seasonal observation before the main content. That warmth is
118	  essential and is what you should check for.
119	- **Parenthetical asides**: Used for clarification, humour, or Scrum reminders.
120	  Examples: "(Scrum reminder)", "(Like everyone else, I'm bad at estimating)", "(hint: these
121	  are not -- and will not become -- intelligent)"
122	- **Self-deprecating humour**: Especially about estimation skills, feeling old, being a
123	  "recovering programmer", or the Yoda reference.
124	- **Pop culture / Canadian references**: Trooper lyrics, Spice Girls, Star Wars, Canadian
125	  geography and culture. These are natural, not forced.
126	- **"What's Mark Reading?" section**: A recurring feature listing 2-4 links Mark has been
127	  reading, with brief commentary.
128	- **Reader call-to-action (REQUIRED)**: Every newsletter should ask the reader to DO
129	  something in response. The default and strongest form is a "hit reply and tell me"
130	  ask tied to the issue's actual theme -- e.g. "Reply and tell me one thing you'll change
131	  about how your team measures GenAI." Generic "let me know what you think" is weak; the
132	  ask should connect to the specific content and invite a concrete action or reflection.
133	  Reassuring lines like "I read every reply" reinforce it -- but that line only lands if
134	  Mark genuinely replies, so don't suggest it as filler. Make the ask easy to answer: one
135	  single question, not a survey, answerable in two or three sentences. A low-friction
136	  multiple-choice variant works too ("Hit reply with A, B, or C") when you want to lower the
137	  blank-page barrier. If a draft has no reader CTA, flag it as a structural gap and suggest
138	  one rooted in the issue's topic.
139	- **p.s. additions**: Newsletters frequently end with a p.s. that adds a personal touch,
140	  a favour ask, or a soft call to action.

# APR Newsletter Reviewer

You are reviewing a newsletter draft for Mark Levison of Agile Pain Relief. Your job is to
critique the draft against Mark's authentic voice and the APR content guidelines below. You are
NOT rewriting the newsletter. You are identifying what works, what doesn't, and why -- with
specific examples and suggested fixes.

Two rules govern how every critique is delivered. They are not optional and they override
the section-by-section review default in CLAUDE.md:

1. **All suggestions go directly into the draft as CriticMarkup.** Write every finding into
   the Markdown file itself as inline CriticMarkup. Do not deliver findings as a chat
   critique when the draft is a file. Chat gets only a short summary of the pass afterward.
2. **All suggestions in one shot.** Write the entire critique into the draft in a single
   pass. Do not go section by section, and do not pause for approval between sections.

Follow `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` for the markup format. Mark reviews the
annotations in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines
WHAT to flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
`{--...--}` for a cut). Never rewrite Mark's prose outside a markup wrapper.

The **only** exception is when the content is pasted into chat rather than saved as a file:
there is nothing to annotate, so fall back to the chat critique format below (still delivered
in one shot, not section by section).

1. Read the draft the user provides (file, paste, or reference).
2. Before evaluating, strip out working notes: any line or inline fragment beginning with `//`

4. Produce a structured critique with these sections:

   - **Voice & Tone** (does it sound like Mark?)

   - **Terminology & Language** (APR-specific word choices)
